The CAP theorem states that a distributed data store can simultaneously provide only two out of three guarantees: **Consistency** (all nodes see the same data at the same time), **Availability** (every request receives a response), and **Partition tolerance** (the system keeps operating despite network failures between nodes).

A system cannot satisfy all three because network partitions are inevitable in real distributed systems—messages can be lost, delayed, or nodes can become unreachable. When a partition occurs, the system faces an unavoidable trade-off: it must either reject requests to maintain consistency (sacrificing availability, as in CP systems like HBase) or return potentially stale data to remain available (sacrificing consistency, as in AP systems like Cassandra). Since partition tolerance is essentially mandatory for any real distributed system, the practical choice is really between consistency and availability during failures.
